after: ## Where the energy goes when you heat something (5.8P)
alt: Energy from heating goes into the thermal store. It either makes the particles move faster, raising the temperature, or overcomes the forces between particles to change the state, with no rise in temperature.
caption: Heating either raises the temperature or changes the state; both increase the stored energy.

alt: Three boxes of particles. A solid has particles packed in regular rows that vibrate in place; a liquid has touching particles in an irregular arrangement; a gas has a few widely spaced particles moving fast in random directions.
caption: Same particles, different arrangement, forces and motion.

alt: Two beakers. In evaporation only the fastest particles at the surface escape, so the liquid left behind has a lower average kinetic energy and cools. In boiling, bubbles of gas form throughout the liquid at the boiling point and the temperature stays constant.
caption: Evaporation: surface only, any temperature, cools the liquid. Boiling: throughout, at the boiling point.

alt: Temperature against time for ice heated at a steady rate. The line rises to 0 °C, stays flat while the ice melts, rises to 100 °C, then stays flat for longer while the water boils.
caption: Flat at 0 °C while melting and at 100 °C while boiling; the boiling section is longer.

alt: Temperature against time for a melted solid cooling in air. The temperature falls, stays flat at the melting point while the substance solidifies, then falls again as the solid cools.
caption: The flat section of a cooling curve is at the melting (freezing) point.

alt: A 2.2 kW kettle holding 0.75 kg of water heated from 15 °C to 100 °C. ΔQ = 0.75 × 4200 × 85 = 267 750 J, and the minimum time is 267 750 ÷ 2200 = 122 s.
caption: Find ΔQ with m × c × ΔT, then divide by the power for the minimum time.

alt: An insulated aluminium block with an electric heater and a thermometer in its holes, a drop of oil around the thermometer bulb. The heater is connected to a power supply with an ammeter in series and a voltmeter across the heater.
caption: Measure I, V and t for the energy, and m and ΔT for the block, then c = E ÷ (m × ΔT).

alt: Worked calculation: E = 4.0 × 12.0 × 300 = 14 400 J, ΔT = 14.4 °C, so c = 1000 J/kg °C. A bar chart compares this with the accepted value of about 900 J/kg °C; the measured value is too high because energy heated the surroundings.
caption: Energy lost to the surroundings makes ΔT too small, so the measured c is too high.
